variants.title: Follow the bundle
variants.context: Every production behavior traces back to an owned project, an immutable bundle, the evidence that approved it, the environment serving it, and a recovery path. Each stage emits a durable artifact that constrains the next: register the project, build reproducibly, promote evidence, then release and operate under bounded exposure.
variants.prompt: A team wants a new model in production on the paved road. Put the platform stages in order.

items.text: Build reproducibly by running versioned code against registered data and feature contracts under one run identity.
Promote evidence by binding model, preprocessing, policy, runtime contract, evaluation results, and signatures to a content-addressed bundle.
Release and operate with shadow or canary policy, observed outcomes, attributed cost, preserved rollback, and auditable retirement.
Register the project with its service owner, workload identities, data class, environments, budgets, and reviewers.

variants.hint: Each stage produces the artifact the next stage is allowed to consume.
variants.explanation: Identity comes first because lineage, evidence, and recovery all attach to it, so an unregistered project has nothing to bind evidence to.

variants.title: Follow the bundle
variants.context: Every production behavior traces back to an owned project, an immutable bundle, the evidence that approved it, the environment serving it, and a recovery path. Each stage emits a durable artifact that constrains the next: register the project, build reproducibly, promote evidence, then release and operate under bounded exposure.
variants.prompt: A specialist workload needs a runtime the paved road does not offer. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Record the measured requirement that the paved road cannot satisfy.
Register the project so ownership, data class, and budgets exist before any exception is discussed.
Approve a reviewed escape hatch that swaps the runtime or scheduler.
Keep project identity, lineage, policy evidence, telemetry, and cost attribution attached to the alternate path.
Operate it under the same bounded exposure, rollback, and incident ownership as any other release.

variants.hint: An escape hatch changes the implementation, not the contract.
variants.explanation: Stranding specialist workloads pushes them off the platform entirely, so the exception preserves the non-negotiable evidence contract instead of dropping it.

variants.title: Follow the bundle
variants.context: Every production behavior traces back to an owned project, an immutable bundle, the evidence that approved it, the environment serving it, and a recovery path. Each stage emits a durable artifact that constrains the next: register the project, build reproducibly, promote evidence, then release and operate under bounded exposure.
variants.prompt: An incident starts and an operator must find who is accountable for a production behavior. Put the trace in order.

items.text: Open the evidence record that approved that bundle, including slice results and approvals.
Read the immutable bundle that digest identifies, with its runtime contract and signatures.
Follow the run lineage back to the code, data, and feature contracts that produced it.
Arrive at the registered project and its accountable service owner.
Start from the serving alias to find the digest the environment is actually routing to.

variants.hint: The trace runs backwards through exactly the artifacts the release created.
variants.explanation: Traceability is only useful in reverse during an incident, which is why identity, lineage, evidence, and recovery are linked rather than merely logged.

variants.title: Move the alias
variants.context: The mutable production alias moves only after four things agree: an immutable candidate bundle with its digest and runtime contract, an evidence record of datasets, slices, safety, latency, cost and approvals, a release policy with traffic cap and stop threshold, and a preserved previous compatible revision.
variants.prompt: A signed candidate with complete lineage is ready for production. Put the release steps in order.

items.text: Move the serving alias to the approved digest and observe within the declared window.
Attach the evidence record with dataset and evaluator versions, slice results, safety tests, latency, and cost.
Confirm the previous compatible revision is still deployable as the rollback target.
Publish the immutable candidate bundle with its content digest, interfaces, and compatibility metadata.
Evaluate the environment's release policy: gates, traffic cap, observation window, and stop threshold.

variants.hint: The alias is a pointer; everything it points at must already be settled.
variants.explanation: The mutable alias moves only after the immutable candidate, evidence record, rollout policy, and rollback target agree.

variants.title: Move the alias
variants.context: The mutable production alias moves only after four things agree: an immutable candidate bundle with its digest and runtime contract, an evidence record of datasets, slices, safety, latency, cost and approvals, a release policy with traffic cap and stop threshold, and a preserved previous compatible revision.
variants.prompt: A candidate has healthy runtime numbers but is unsigned and its data-to-evaluator lineage is incomplete. Put what happens in order.

items.text: The policy returns every blocker at once rather than failing on the first one.
The team repairs lineage and signing and resubmits the same digest for evaluation.
The alias stays on the current revision, so no traffic is exposed.
The candidate bundle is published and its digest is computed.
The evidence check finds the missing signature and the incomplete lineage.

variants.hint: Good runtime numbers are one gate among several, not a substitute for the others.
variants.explanation: An evidence-grade record binds artifact identity and lineage alongside metrics, so healthy latency cannot compensate for an unbound artifact.

variants.title: Move the alias
variants.context: The mutable production alias moves only after four things agree: an immutable candidate bundle with its digest and runtime contract, an evidence record of datasets, slices, safety, latency, cost and approvals, a release policy with traffic cap and stop threshold, and a preserved previous compatible revision.
variants.prompt: A canary crosses its stop threshold ten minutes into the observation window. Put the recovery steps in order.

items.text: Exposure ends and the incident is attributed to the owning team named in the project.
The observed metric crosses the machine-readable stop threshold for that environment.
The controller halts the rollout instead of continuing to the next traffic step.
The blocking evidence is recorded against that digest so the same bundle cannot be promoted unchanged.
The alias is pointed back at the previous compatible revision.

variants.hint: Recovery is a declared path with an owner, not an improvised decision.
variants.explanation: Rollback thresholds are machine-readable and the previous revision stays deployable, which is what makes exposure reversible within the observation window.

variants.title: Choose isolation by consequence
variants.context: Isolation is chosen by consequence, not by namespace habit. Each workload declares a minimum isolation score and control coverage from its trust level and data class, and each sharing pattern offers a measured score, coverage, packing efficiency, and blast radius.
variants.prompt: A customer-facing GenAI workload on confidential data requires an isolation score of at least 72 and control coverage of at least 82 percent. A shared namespace pool measures 58 and 76 percent, a virtual control plane measures 82 and 89 percent. Which pattern should be selected?
options: The shared namespace pool, since quotas and network policy can be configured around it.
The virtual control plane, since it clears both declared minimums.
A dedicated cluster, since more isolation is always the safer choice.
optionFeedback: It measures below both declared minimums, so configuration would have to make up a gap that was already quantified.
Correct: the pattern is chosen because it meets the isolation and coverage the consequence declared.
It clears the bar but buys isolation this consequence did not require, at a much worse packing and cost envelope.
variants.hint: The workload already declared its minimums; compare them against the measured pattern.
variants.explanation: Isolation is selected against declared minimums for trust, data consequence, and failure radius rather than by habit or by always maximizing.

variants.title: Choose isolation by consequence
variants.context: Isolation is chosen by consequence, not by namespace habit. Each workload declares a minimum isolation score and control coverage from its trust level and data class, and each sharing pattern offers a measured score, coverage, packing efficiency, and blast radius.
variants.prompt: A regulated decision-support workload processes restricted data and needs separately auditable production change control. Which pattern fits?
options: A namespace with strict quotas, since quotas bound the noisy-neighbor effect.
A virtual control plane, since tenant API resources are already separated.
A dedicated production cluster, so change control and failure radius are separable.
optionFeedback: Quotas address fairness, not the audit and failure-radius requirements of restricted data.
Separate API resources still leave shared workers and shared upgrade risk in the blast radius.
Correct: restricted data with auditable change control needs a boundary that is not shared with other tenants.
variants.hint: Ask which failures and which change windows this workload is allowed to share.
variants.explanation: A virtual control plane separates tenant API resources but keeps shared workers and failure modes, which a separately auditable regulated workload cannot accept.

variants.title: Choose isolation by consequence
variants.context: Isolation is chosen by consequence, not by namespace habit. Each workload declares a minimum isolation score and control coverage from its trust level and data class, and each sharing pattern offers a measured score, coverage, packing efficiency, and blast radius.
variants.prompt: Trusted employees run interruptible training and notebook jobs on non-production data, and the platform wants maximum accelerator packing. Which pattern fits?
options: A dedicated cluster per team, so nobody waits behind another team's job.
A virtual control plane, so each team gets its own API surface.
A shared namespace pool, since the declared minimums are low and packing is best.
optionFeedback: Dedicated clusters for interruptible internal work spend isolation budget where there is no consequence to protect.
Separate API surfaces add control-plane overhead that this trust level and data class do not require.
Correct: trusted tenants on non-production data have low declared minimums, so the pattern with the strongest packing wins.
variants.hint: Low consequence is a real input, not an excuse to skip the declaration.
variants.explanation: Sharing is chosen from trust, data consequence, fairness, and failure radius together, so a low-consequence workload can take the densest pattern deliberately.

variants.title: Map the four planes
variants.context: Four planes hold durable responsibilities. The developer plane turns intent into reviewable configuration. The control plane reconciles identity, quota, lineage, and release policy. The data and execution plane runs bounded work. The evidence plane keeps outcomes linked to project and artifact identity.
variants.prompt: Match each platform plane to the responsibility it owns.

pairs.label: Developer plane
pairs.detail: Turns a project request into reviewable configuration through templates, APIs, and a portal.

pairs.label: Control plane
pairs.detail: Validates identity, quotas, lineage, evaluation, release policy, and desired state.

pairs.label: Data and execution plane
pairs.detail: Runs pipelines, training, registries, and serving under declared resource and access limits.

pairs.label: Evidence plane
pairs.detail: Keeps metrics, approvals, cost, incidents, and retirements linked to project and artifact identity.

variants.hint: Ask which plane would have to change to answer each question differently.
variants.explanation: The planes are contracts rather than products, which is why a portal alone is not the platform and the contract must survive across every system.

variants.context: Four planes hold durable responsibilities. The developer plane turns intent into reviewable configuration. The control plane reconciles identity, quota, lineage, and release policy. The data and execution plane runs bounded work. The evidence plane keeps outcomes linked to project and artifact identity.
variants.prompt: Match each artifact to the plane that produces it.

pairs.label: A reviewable project contract in version control
pairs.detail: Where teams declare intent instead of triggering hidden automation.

pairs.label: A precise policy failure naming the unmet gate
pairs.detail: Where desired state is reconciled against declared rules.

pairs.label: A training run under a quota-bounded accelerator pool
A cost figure attributed to an owning team
pairs.detail: Where outcomes stay linked to identity.

variants.hint: Follow the artifact back to the system that had to exist for it to be produced.
variants.explanation: Each plane emits artifacts the others consume, so hiding generated configuration or losing attribution breaks the chain rather than simplifying it.

The data and execution plane runs bounded work. The evidence plane keeps outcomes linked to project and artifact identity.
variants.prompt: Match each failure symptom to the plane that broke.

pairs.label: Teams abandon the paved road because intent cannot be expressed
pairs.detail: The declaration surface is not usable.

pairs.label: A workload deploys without a service owner or quota
pairs.detail: Reconciliation is not enforcing the declared rules.

pairs.label: One tenant's burst starves another team's training queue
pairs.detail: Bounded execution limits are not holding.

pairs.label: An incident cannot be attributed to a project or artifact
pairs.detail: Observed outcomes are no longer linked to identity.

variants.hint: Each symptom names a promise the platform made and did not keep.
variants.explanation: Platform health is measured by whether teams reach a safe production state and recover, so symptoms are traced to the plane whose contract failed.

variants.title: Read the release gate
variants.context: Release gates are numeric and machine-readable. A quality delta must clear zero, the critical slice must stay above its floor of -0.5 percent, the error-rate delta must stay under 0.2 points, and the p95 latency delta must stay under 20 ms, while a canary caps how much traffic is exposed.
variants.prompt: A bounded canary is set to 10 percent of a 6,000 requests-per-second production baseline. How many requests per second reach the candidate?
variants.hint: Exposure is the share of live traffic the policy allows, not the whole baseline.
variants.explanation: The traffic cap is what bounds user exposure during the observation window, so the canary serves 10 percent of the baseline rate.

mistakes.feedback: That is the full baseline; the canary caps exposure below it.
That is the traffic still served by the incumbent revision.

variants.title: Read the release gate
variants.context: Release gates are numeric and machine-readable. A quality delta must clear zero, the critical slice must stay above its floor of -0.5 percent, the error-rate delta must stay under 0.2 points, and the p95 latency delta must stay under 20 ms, while a canary caps how much traffic is exposed.
variants.prompt: The critical-slice floor is -0.5 percent. A candidate improves aggregate quality but regresses the critical slice by 2.6 percent. By how many percentage points does it miss the floor?
variants.hint: Measure the distance from the floor, not the size of the regression.
variants.explanation: The slice sits 2.1 points below its floor, and an aggregate gain does not buy back a critical-slice regression that the gate declared unacceptable.

mistakes.feedback: That adds the two magnitudes instead of measuring the distance from the floor.
That is the regression itself, not the amount by which it misses the floor.

variants.title: Read the release gate
variants.context: Release gates are numeric and machine-readable. A quality delta must clear zero, the critical slice must stay above its floor of -0.5 percent, the error-rate delta must stay under 0.2 points, and the p95 latency delta must stay under 20 ms, while a canary caps how much traffic is exposed.
variants.prompt: The gate allows a p95 latency delta of at most 20 ms. A candidate measures a delta of 14 ms. How much headroom is left against that gate?
variants.hint: Headroom is what remains before the declared limit is reached.
variants.explanation: Headroom is the gate limit minus the measured delta, and it is what tells the owner how much regression a later change can still absorb.

mistakes.feedback: That adds the measurement to the limit instead of subtracting it.
That is the candidate's measured delta, not the remaining headroom.
